title: Efficient Scene-Text Refinementvia Pixel-Space Grouped Image Generation

paper.title: Efficient Scene-Text Refinement via Pixel-Space Grouped Image Generation
paper.abstract: Abstract Generated images often have coherent layouts and visual content, yet local errors in small text and complex characters still limit their readability and practical use. Scene-text refinement requires accuracy , preservation , and efficiency . Existing methods based on variational autoencoders (VAEs) can lose fine strokes during reconstruction, while full-image editing can shift background colors. In this work, we introduce PixText , a model that formulates local text refinement as grouped image generation in pixel space. Conditioned on the original image, PixText generates only the target regions, preserves unedited content, and uses MeanFlow for four-step generation. We further introduce Text Refinement Bench to evaluate text correction and image preservation in generated images. On this benchmark, PixText achieves 83.06% glyph pass and 94.66% exact target-character OCR accuracy, versus 36.77% and 52.31% for the strongest baseline. Its four-step MeanFlow variant retains an 81.84% pass rate with less than one GPU-second of amortized generation cost per image.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large text-to-image models have made rapid progress in text rendering and layout. Images often exhibit reasonable layouts and mostly correct text, yet errors persist in small text and complex characters. These errors occupy only a small part of an image but directly affect its readability and practical usability. Further improving text accuracy within a general-purpose generative model requires balancing text fidelity against overall visual quality. For example, the pretraining experience of LongCat-Image shows that synthetic text data improves text accuracy but can impair overall visual coherence, motivating dynamic adjustment of its sampling proportion and its removal toward the end of pretraining ( Team et al., 2025 ) . Post-training for text accuracy faces a similar challenge: excessive optimization of text rewards can make text disproportionately large or prominent, compromising aesthetics and visual coherence ( Diao et al., 2026 ; Team et al., 2026 ; Mao et al., 2026b ; Jin et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026a ; Kang et al., 2026 ) . These observations motivate separating text refinement from overall image generation : preserving the layout, style, and visual content produced by the base model while precisely correcting only the erroneous text regions. Scene-text refinement calls for accuracy, preservation, and efficiency : correcting text faithfully, leaving unedited content unchanged, and keeping computational cost low. Existing text generation and editing methods, however, typically redraw entire text regions and can alter their original layout, style, and typeface. Most build on large latent-space generative models ( Tuo et al., 2024b ; Tuo et al., 2024a ; Lan et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) , whose ability to generate and refine small text is constrained by variational autoencoder (VAE) reconstruction ( Yu et al., 2026 ) , while also incurring the cost of a large generative network and VAE encoding and decoding. Applying these methods directly to localized corrections of a few characters therefore makes it difficult to satisfy all three requirements. To tackle these challenges, we introduce PixText , a text generation and refinement model based on grouped image generation in pixel space. First, we model images directly in pixel space, removing the VAE reconstruction bottleneck for small-character strokes as well as the texture degradation and color shifts introduced by local encoding and decoding. Second, we use the original image as the source that provides context and organize the regions to be refined as a group of image elements. The model predicts only the item pixels, which are then pasted back into the original image. By avoiding full-image regeneration, this design preserves unedited regions and reduces the background color drift and paste seams introduced by full-image generation. Finally, four-step MeanFlow ( Geng et al., 2026a ) reduces amortized generation cost to less than one GPU-second per image. Meanwhile, we propose simple, effective training and inference improvements. We identify the influence of the training timestep distribution on patch-boundary artifacts and mitigate them with uniform sampling, observing consistent improvements in our model and MiniT2I ( Wang et al., 2026d ) . We also revise the x x -prediction sampling update to reduce speckle from incomplete denoising. As a final contribution, we propose a new benchmark for text refinement. The existing AnyText Bench ( Tuo et al., 2024b ) primarily evaluates conventional text generation and lacks a dedicated evaluation of localized text errors in generated images. We therefore construct Text Refinement Bench from model-generated images, providing character-level error annotations, correction targets, and a unified evaluation protocol. The benchmark evaluates correction accuracy, background preservation, and inference efficiency. Experiments show that PixText outperforms existing baselines on text refinement and achieves performance close to or above the best existing methods on AnyText Bench at lower computational cost.

sections.heading: 2.1 Scene-Text Generation and Editing
sections.text: Early scene-text editing methods modeled content and style to replace text while preserving its appearance ( Wu et al., 2019 ; Roy et al., 2020 ; Yang et al., 2020 ; Krishnan et al., 2023 ; Lee et al., 2021 ; Qu et al., 2023 ) . Diffusion models improved text generation and editing through layout, glyph, and character conditioning ( Chen et al., 2023b ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2023 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024a ; Liu et al., 2024b ; Tuo et al., 2024b ; Tuo et al., 2024a ; Ji et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023a ; Zhao and Lian, 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) . Subsequent work advanced glyph accuracy, style control, and multilingual editing ( Zeng et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Yan et al., 2025 ; Fang et al., 2025 ; Lan et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026c ) , extending to open-vocabulary, training-free, and instruction-driven unified text editing ( Li et al., 2026a ; Gunawan et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026c ; Wang et al., 2026c ; Ma et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026a ) , as well as text correction in generated images ( Shimoda et al., 2025 ) . We focus on refining a few erroneous characters in generated images: jointly generating multiple target regions directly in pixel space avoids the effects of VAE compression and reconstruction on fine strokes while preserving unedited content. Four-step MeanFlow improves efficiency while keeping the amortized generation cost below one GPU-second per image.

sections.heading: 2.2 Pixel-Space Generation
sections.text: Pixel-space generation models images directly, avoiding information loss from latent compression. Early work explored high-resolution modeling and computational efficiency ( Hoogeboom et al., 2023 ; Hoogeboom et al., 2025 ; Jabri et al., 2022 ; Crowson et al., 2024 ; Atzmon et al., 2024 ) , while subsequent methods improved quality and efficiency through global–local modeling and frequency decomposition ( Chen et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Yu et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026e ; Ma et al., 2026b ; Lin et al., 2026a ) . JiT demonstrated the effectiveness of predicting clean images directly ( Li and He, 2026 ) ; related studies explored perceptual supervision, generative trajectories, and text-to-image generation and editing ( Ma et al., 2026c ; Baade et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026d ; Cai et al., 2026 ) , while transferring pretrained latent-space models reduced training costs ( Chen et al., 2026d ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) . Meanwhile, MeanFlow and its successors model average velocity for few-step generation, extending this approach to pixel space ( Geng et al., 2026a ; Geng et al., 2026b ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . Building on these advances, we focus on local text refinement conditioned on the original image, jointly generating the target regions to combine glyph accuracy, content preservation, and efficiency.

sections.heading: 3.1 Pixel-Space Generation for Quality and Efficiency
sections.text: Latent-space text generation and editing methods rely on VAE compression and reconstruction ( Li et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2023b ; Zeng et al., 2024 ; Tuo et al., 2024b ; Tuo et al., 2024a ; Lan et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) , which can lose fine strokes and incur additional decoding cost. Related work on autoregressive models also identifies visual-tokenizer reconstruction as a bottleneck for text detail and improves glyph quality by enhancing the decoder ( Mao et al., 2026a ) . In Figure 2 , a character approximately 20 pixels high becomes difficult to recognize after reconstruction with Stable Diffusion, FLUX.1, and Qwen-Image VAEs ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Labs et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) . For edits involving only a few characters, decoding only the target region may lower VAE decoding cost, but the smaller region gives the decoder less image context. Figure 3 compares full-image and local FLUX.1-VAE decoding from the same latent representation obtained by encoding the full image: the independently decoded region exhibits a visible color mismatch when pasted back, even with 32 pixels of additional context. Figure 2: Small-character degradation during VAE reconstruction. Each VAE uses full-image encoding and posterior-mode decoding in FP32. Figure 3: Local FLUX.1-VAE decoding causes visible color shifts when pasted back into the original image, even with 32 pixels of context. We therefore build a flow matching model directly in pixel space, eliminating VAE encoding and decoding, and adopt the simple JiT architecture ( Li and He, 2026 ) . Table 1 shows that, under matched hardware and resolution, a single call to the JiT-L/16 output head takes less than 1% of the decoding time of the evaluated autoencoders, which also include FLUX.2 and DC-AE ( Labs, 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025a ) . Among pixel-space models, its output head is also lighter than those of PixelDiT, DiP, and DeCo ( Yu et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026e ; Ma et al., 2026b ) . These heads run at every denoising step, so their costs accumulate across sampling steps, motivating us to retain JiT’s lightweight design. sections.heading: 3.2 Text Editing and Refinement as Grouped Image Generation
sections.text: Figure 4: Color preservation and grid-artifact mitigation. (a) Full images, local close-ups, and color-gradient maps, with background color-error distributions. (b) Generated images and color-gradient maps before and after uniform sampling, with PixText and MiniT2I boundary-gradient curves. Heatmaps share a scale within each panel; shading denotes 95% bootstrap intervals. Recent scene-text editing methods ( Lan et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ) use full-image inpainting: even for local text edits, they update and decode full-image latents, reconstructing background that requires no modification. This full-image generation can shift background colors, leaving visible seams after crop-and-paste editing ( Figure 4 (a) ). The shift exceeds the VAE-only reconstruction error, showing that pasting alone does not ensure color consistency between the edited region and the original image. We formulate text editing and refinement as grouped image generation in pixel space, separating context from generation targets. During both training and inference, we erase the existing text in each target region through local blurring before using the source image as the main-image condition. The resulting image serves as a main image providing context, while each region to be edited forms an item image . The model predicts only the item pixels and pastes them into the original. The extent of generation therefore follows the size of the edit regions, while pixels outside them are retained directly. We denote the N N clean items by x 1 = { x 1 i } i = 1 N x_{1}=\{x_{1}^{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} and their noisy counterparts by z t = { z t i } i = 1 N z_{t}=\{z_{t}^{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} . Conditioned on the main image and target glyph images, denoted by c c , the model jointly predicts x ^ 1 = f θ ​ ( z t , t , c ) \hat{x}_{1}=f_{\theta}(z_{t},t,c) . The input comprises main-image, noisy item-image, and glyph-image tokens, which provide scene context, represent generation targets, and specify text content, respectively. At sampling time, item images are initialized from 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{N}(0,I) . Main and item images share an RGB embedder. Glyph images are rendered with PIL in single-channel grayscale and mapped to the same feature dimension through a separate glyph embedder. Target text is specified entirely through these glyph images, removing the need to deploy an additional text encoder. As illustrated in Figure 1 (b) , we use Centered Continuous Position Encoding (CCPE) to align the main image and independently cropped items across scales in the coordinate system of the original image. Let the original image have size H × W H\times W , the patch size be p p , and ( y , x ) (y,x) denote a patch center in original-image pixel coordinates. Its 3D RoPE coordinates ( Su et al., 2024 ) are 𝝅 = ( n , y − H / 2 p , x − W / 2 p ) , n = { 0 , main image , 1 , item image , 2 , glyph image . \bm{\pi}=\left(n,\frac{y-H/2}{p},\frac{x-W/2}{p}\right),\qquad n=\begin{cases}0,&\text{main image},\\ 1,&\text{item image},\\ 2,&\text{glyph image}.\end{cases} (3) Each glyph shares the spatial coordinates of its paired item and is distinguished by the role coordinate n n . Continuous spatial coordinates allow item crops to start at arbitrary pixel locations without aligning to the main-image patch grid. Only crop dimensions need to be expanded to multiples of p p , avoiding extra padding from grid alignment. Across 116,038 text regions, this reduces the number of item tokens by 13.7% relative to grid-aligned crops; Appendix E provides the comparison. We adapt JiT blocks for grouped image generation and call the resulting blocks Group JiT Blocks . These tokens are jointly processed by 32 such blocks. As illustrated in Figure 1 (c) , the main image and items interact bidirectionally, and different items attend to one another to share scene information and editing context. Cross-image attention involving each glyph is restricted to bidirectional interaction with its paired item, preserving the correspondence between text conditions and editing targets. We inject timestep conditions through adaLN-Zero ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) : noisy items receive the current timestep t t , while the main image and glyphs use the fixed clean endpoint t = 1 t=1 , distinguishing generation targets from known conditions. We use FlexAttention ( Dong et al., 2024 ) to batch variable-length image groups; implementation details are provided in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 3.3 Training and Sampling
sections.text: We train PixText directly for local text editing, conditioning on the main image and glyphs while adding noise to and predicting only the item images. We choose the editing granularity according to the writing system, using character-level regions for Chinese and word-level regions for alphabetic writing systems such as English to support fine-grained refinement. Glyph conditions are rendered from the recognized text. Training uses the noise path and velocity-space objective in Section 3.1 . We average the loss over pixels and channels within each item, then equally over items: ℒ = 𝔼 x 1 , c , t , ϵ ​ [ 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N ‖ v ^ t i − v t ∗ , i ‖ 2 2 D i ] , \mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}_{x_{1},c,t,\epsilon}\!\left[\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{\|\hat{v}_{t}^{i}-v_{t}^{*,i}\|_{2}^{2}}{D_{i}}\right], (4) where D i D_{i} is the number of scalar pixel values in item i i . Grid artifacts aligned with patch boundaries have been observed across JiT-based pixel-space models ( Wang et al., 2026d ; Jiang et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ) . We find that these artifacts can be mitigated by a simple change to the training timestep distribution. After initial training with logit-normal sampling, we switch to uniform sampling and continue training. Generated images and color-gradient maps in Figure 4 (b) show weaker patch-boundary discontinuities after uniform sampling; the bottom-left plot compares both training strategies from the same initialization. Uniform sampling yields lower patch-boundary gradients at both continuation checkpoints, indicating weaker grid artifacts. We further evaluate this strategy on MiniT2I-B/16. Starting from the same pretrained checkpoint used for the official logit-normal fine-tuning, we adopt uniform timestep sampling during post-training without modifying the architecture. The bottom-right plot in Figure 4 (b) shows lower boundary gradients than the official logit-normal fine-tuned model across all five inference schedules, indicating that this simple post-training adjustment also mitigates grid artifacts in another pixel-space model. Appendix F provides the experimental details. The sampling implementations of JiT and MiniT2I impose a lower bound on 1 − t 1-t when converting clean-image predictions into velocities, preventing the denominator from approaching zero near the denoising endpoint ( Li and He, 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026d ) . We observe that this floor can weaken the final updates and leave residual speckle. We instead formulate the update directly in terms of the clean prediction, so the final step returns it in full. We hold the main-image and glyph conditions c c fixed and initialize the items from Gaussian noise, z 0 i ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) z_{0}^{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) . sections.heading: 3.4 Efficient Generation with MeanFlow
sections.text: To reduce the number of sampling steps, we distill a trained PixText teacher using MeanFlow to learn the average velocity over a time interval ( Geng et al., 2026a ) . We observe low-precision derivative errors in reference implementations and our own model, and therefore use higher precision for derivative estimation while retaining low-precision computation elsewhere in training to control the additional cost. sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: AnyText Bench focuses on reconstructing annotated text at specified locations ( Tuo et al., 2024b ) , leaving a gap in open, reproducible evaluation of localized text refinement on generated images. We therefore construct Text Refinement Bench from actual model-generated images, including those released in the public Qwen-Image Bench ( Li et al., 2026b ) . Human review verifies erroneous character regions and correction targets and excludes invalid cases before freezing the evaluation list, directly reflecting the practical need to correct local errors while preserving the original image. The benchmark evaluates correction accuracy and image preservation on 1,034 images with 2,638 repair targets. We also evaluate text reconstruction on the Chinese and English subsets of AnyText Bench to assess performance on conventional visual text generation. During evaluation, we identify inaccurate text polygons and failures of the original OCR evaluation pipeline on vertically arranged text. We correct the affected text regions and adapt OCR preprocessing for vertical layouts, reducing scoring errors caused by cropping and text orientation so that evaluation better reflects the quality of the generated text. Standard OCR may transcribe a generated glyph with missing or extra strokes as the intended character, so correct recognition does not necessarily imply a successful repair. We therefore use CJK-CLIP, a dedicated CLIP-style glyph recognizer for characters, 1 1 1 The work presenting CJK-CLIP is currently under review; the model will be publicly released. to distinguish correct glyphs from visually similar but structurally incorrect outputs for character-level evaluation on Text Refinement Bench. Appendix D further describes the benchmark, its differences from related benchmarks, and the evaluation protocol.

sections.heading: Implementation details.
sections.text: We train the model on eight H800 GPUs using an internal Chinese–English dataset containing approximately 2.53 million image records. Base-model training uses AdamW with a learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} , β = ( 0.9 , 0.95 ) \beta=(0.9,0.95) , zero weight decay, and an EMA decay of 0.9999. Each optimizer reinitialization starts with 2,000 linear warmup steps, followed by a constant learning rate. We follow a progressive-resolution schedule: we first train for approximately 13 epochs with at most 512 2 512^{2} pixels per main image, then increase this limit to 1024 2 1024^{2} and continue training for approximately 15 epochs. We subsequently perform approximately 3,000 MeanFlow updates with an effective batch size of 24. PixText uses patch size p = 16 p=16 , 32 Group JiT Blocks, hidden dimension 1280, and 16 attention heads. The denominator floor for velocity conversion is δ = 0.05 \delta=0.05 . Initial logit-normal timestep sampling uses μ = − 0.8 \mu=-0.8 and σ = 0.8 \sigma=0.8 , followed by uniform sampling. MeanFlow uses the same optimizer settings. Both the student and frozen teacher are initialized from the base model’s EMA weights, and training intervals are formed by sorting two independently sampled uniform timesteps. The default DDE step size is h = 0.005 h=0.005 , reduced near boundaries as described above. Finite-difference predictions and subtraction use FP32 tensor arithmetic, with TF32 enabled for matrix multiplications; the trainable student forward and backward passes use BF16 mixed precision. For the main-table evaluation, PixText uses 25 Euler steps and MeanFlow uses four Euler steps, both with a glyph-conditioned classifier-free guidance (CFG) ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) scale of 3.3 (see Appendix B for details).

sections.heading: 4.2 Quantitative Comparisons
sections.text: Table 2 compares eight text-specialized methods with PixText and its four-step MeanFlow variant. On Text Refinement Bench, PixText achieves a Pass of 83.06%, compared with 36.77% for the strongest baseline, FLUX-Text, while also attaining the lowest FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) and LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) . PP-OCRv6 gives PixText 94.66% exact target-character accuracy, compared with 52.31% for FLUX-Text. On AnyText Bench, PixText achieves the highest Chinese text accuracy and ranks second to FLUX-Text on English, showing that its refinement advantage is accompanied by competitive text reconstruction. For each Chinese-capable baseline, we report the complete line- or character-input run with higher text accuracy; Table 4 reports both settings and all four metrics. The four-step MeanFlow variant retains the refinement advantage over the baselines while reducing generation cost relative to the base PixText model, making localized correction practical in generation workflows. sections.text: Figure 6 compares six localized text refinement or generation cases across lettering styles and backgrounds. At matched scales, PixText and its four-step MeanFlow variant produce legible text while preserving local appearance; some baselines distort strokes, style, or nearby content. Appendix G gives fourteen more cases, and Appendix H shows glyph-conditioned generation beyond the main Chinese–English training scripts.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: PixText refines text through localized pixel-space grouped generation, preserving fine strokes and surrounding content. It substantially improves correction on Text Refinement Bench, while its four-step MeanFlow variant costs less than one amortized GPU-second per image. Targeted pixel-space generation thus improves text readability while preserving image appearance.

sections.heading: Appendix A Variable-Length Batch Training with FlexAttention
sections.text: The main-image resolution, number of edit regions, and region sizes vary across samples, giving each image group a different number of tokens. We concatenate the main-image, item-image, and glyph tokens from all groups along the sequence dimension to form a batch, without padding each group to a common length. Each token retains its group membership and spatial position within the group, allowing samples with different image sizes and numbers of regions to be trained together. The attention mask controls both isolation between groups and interaction within each group. Attention between different groups is fully masked. Within a group, the main image and items interact bidirectionally, items attend to one another, and each glyph interacts across images only with its paired item; self-attention within each image is retained. Sequence concatenation therefore changes how the batch is organized while preserving the information flow within each sample. We encode these rules as a FlexAttention block-sparse mask and reuse it across Transformer layers. FlexAttention skips fully masked attention blocks and applies the specified masking within the remaining blocks, without explicitly storing a dense attention matrix for the entire concatenated sequence. Combining variable-length sequence packing with masked attention avoids the computation introduced by padding to the longest sample, while preserving joint modeling within groups and independence between groups.

sections.heading: Condition dropout.
sections.text: We train the two classifier-free guidance (CFG) branches by randomly dropping glyph conditions. For each training image group, we remove all glyph tokens associated with its items with probability 0.1; otherwise, all glyph conditions are retained. Dropping a condition removes the glyph branch from the input sequence. The main image, noisy items, and region geometry remain available, so “unconditional” here refers only to the absence of target glyphs; scene context is still provided. Random condition dropout is disabled during validation and inference, when predictions with and without glyph conditions are constructed explicitly.

sections.heading: Inference guidance.
sections.text: We separate the retained scene and geometry conditions c ctx c_{\mathrm{ctx}} from the glyph conditions g g . Let x ^ 1 cond = f θ ​ ( z t , t , c ctx , g ) \hat{x}_{1}^{\mathrm{cond}}=f_{\theta}(z_{t},t,c_{\mathrm{ctx}},g) and x ^ 1 uncond = f θ ​ ( z t , t , c ctx , ∅ ) \hat{x}_{1}^{\mathrm{uncond}}=f_{\theta}(z_{t},t,c_{\mathrm{ctx}},\emptyset) . The guided clean-item prediction is x ^ 1 CFG = x ^ 1 uncond + γ ⁡ ( t ) ​ ( x ^ 1 cond − x ^ 1 uncond ) . \hat{x}_{1}^{\mathrm{CFG}}=\hat{x}_{1}^{\mathrm{uncond}}+\gamma(t)\bigl(\hat{x}_{1}^{\mathrm{cond}}-\hat{x}_{1}^{\mathrm{uncond}}\bigr). (10) Both predictions share the noisy state, timestep, main image, and region positions. By default, the sampler uses the specified guidance scale for 0.1 < t < 1 0.1<t<1 and sets γ ⁡ ( t ) = 1 \gamma(t)=1 otherwise, returning the conditional prediction directly. The main-table guidance scale is 3.3.

sections.heading: Use in MeanFlow.
sections.text: MeanFlow training retains the same group-level glyph dropout, and the teacher and student receive the same glyph-condition state. The teacher predicts the target instantaneous velocity under the sampled glyph-condition state. At inference, both branches share the interval start t t and endpoint s s . Their interval-conditioned clean predictions are combined as above and then converted to average velocity. Because both branches share the noisy state and velocity-conversion denominator, this is equivalent to u θ CFG = u θ uncond + γ ⁡ ( t ) ​ ( u θ cond − u θ uncond ) , u_{\theta}^{\mathrm{CFG}}=u_{\theta}^{\mathrm{uncond}}+\gamma(t)\bigl(u_{\theta}^{\mathrm{cond}}-u_{\theta}^{\mathrm{uncond}}\bigr), (11) followed by an Euler update. Thus, four steps denotes four interval updates; steps with CFG enabled require separate predictions with and without glyph conditions.

sections.heading: Appendix C Precision and Efficiency of MeanFlow DDE
sections.text: DDE estimates derivatives by subtracting nearby predictions, making the estimate sensitive to the numerical precision of endpoint evaluation. We use FP32 tensors for endpoint predictions and subtraction, enable TF32 matrix multiplications, and retain BF16 computation for the trainable center forward and backward passes. We compare BF16, strict FP32, and our mixed-precision endpoint computation on the MeanFlow model used in the main results, using three training samples with a fixed interval ( t , s ) = ( 0.4 , 0.8 ) (t,s)=(0.4,0.8) and finite-difference step size h = 0.005 h=0.005 . The reference D FP32 D_{\mathrm{FP32}} is the finite-difference estimate computed in strict FP32 with TF32 disabled; relative error is ‖ D − D FP32 ‖ 2 / ‖ D FP32 ‖ 2 \|D-D_{\mathrm{FP32}}\|_{2}/\|D_{\mathrm{FP32}}\|_{2} . Timing on dedicated NVIDIA H800 GPUs covers derivative estimation, the center forward pass, loss computation, and backward propagation, with two warm-up runs followed by seven measurements per configuration. Table 3: DDE precision and efficiency. All configurations use BF16 center forward and backward passes and differ only in endpoint computation. We report medians over three samples, taking the median of seven timing measurements for each sample. Endpoint computation Relative error (%) ↓ \downarrow Time (s) ↓ \downarrow BF16 192.64 0.551 Strict FP32 (reference) 0.00 23.895 Ours (mixed precision) 18.92 0.706 Table 3 shows that our mixed-precision scheme reduces the median relative derivative error from 192.64% to 18.92%, with only 28% more computation time than BF16, while running approximately 34 × 34\times faster than strict FP32. This supports concentrating higher precision on derivative estimation to reduce finite-difference error while keeping computation efficient.

sections.heading: Comparison with existing benchmarks.
sections.text: Text Refinement Bench targets local character errors in generated images, complementing text-generation benchmarks such as AnyText ( Tuo et al., 2024b ) and instruction-driven editing benchmarks such as TextEdit, TextEditBench, and MultiTextEdit ( Tian et al., 2026 ; Gui et al., 2025 ; Cheng et al., 2026 ) . Explicit repair regions and target characters focus evaluation on correction quality and image preservation, reducing dependence on instruction interpretation and target localization. ScenePair ( Zeng et al., 2024 ) also provides region-level pairs, but its source text and target reference come from the same image. Although its original crop-based protocol does not expose the reference, directly supplying the full image as context would reveal it; evaluating context-aware refinement therefore requires adapting this setup. Our benchmark is built around repairing actual generation errors with the surrounding image as context, and jointly measures target-glyph agreement, character identification, and image preservation.

sections.heading: Evaluation set.
sections.text: The reviewed benchmark contains 1,034 images and 2,638 repair targets. All methods use all 2,638 repair targets for character-level metrics, and FID and LPIPS cover the same 1,034 images.

sections.heading: Evaluating glyph correctness.
sections.text: We use CJK-CLIP to measure similarity between a character image and its intended character, evaluating glyph correctness beyond whether the image can be recognized as the target.

sections.heading: Pass and R@1.
sections.text: All methods are evaluated with the same CJK-CLIP model and character-specific pass thresholds. Let S ⁡ ( I , y ) S(I,y) denote the similarity between character image I I and target y y , and let μ y \mu_{y} be its mean over reference images of that character. A repaired glyph passes when pass ( I , y ) = [ S ( I , y ) ≥ μ y − 0.03 ] . \operatorname{pass}(I,y)=\mathbb{1}\!\left[S(I,y)\geq\mu_{y}-0.03\right]. (12) Pass is the fraction of target characters satisfying this criterion; R@1 is the fraction for which the target ranks first by similarity over the character vocabulary. They measure target-glyph agreement and character identification, respectively. A malformed glyph can still be closest to the intended character, explaining why R@1 can exceed Pass. AnyText Bench retains its OCR-based evaluation.

sections.heading: OCR check.
sections.text: We additionally evaluate the same 2,638 target characters with the PP-OCRv6 medium recognizer. 2 2 2 https://huggingface.co/PaddlePaddle/PP-OCRv6_medium_rec OCR Acc is the percentage whose transcription exactly matches the repair target; blank or multi-character outputs count as errors. OCR Acc measures recognizability, whereas Pass additionally tests glyph fidelity. Figure 7 illustrates stroke errors missed by high-confidence OCR recognition. All four glyphs are transcribed as their targets with confidence between 99.67% and 99.97%, yet fail the CJK-CLIP criterion, consistent with the human error annotations. Figure 7: Correct recognition does not imply correct glyphs. OCR confidently transcribes these malformed glyphs as the targets above, CJK-CLIP similarity scores fall below their respective acceptance thresholds μ y − 0.03 \mu_{y}-0.03 , yielding Error decisions consistent with human annotations.

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: Pass, R@1, and OCR Acc on Text Refinement Bench, and sentence accuracy (Acc) on AnyText, are reported as percentages. LPIPS uses AlexNet on full images resized to 256 × 256 256\times 256 . Chinese AnyText OCR scores use a common set of vertical text boxes and symbol-width equivalence rules.

sections.heading: AnyText evaluation corrections.
sections.text: Some original polygons do not accurately cover the text, so direct cropping can truncate glyphs or include neighboring content. We review the character boxes and use the corrected regions for vertically arranged Chinese text. Characters are cropped in top-to-bottom reading order, kept upright, and concatenated horizontally before OCR, avoiding recognition errors caused by rotating the entire vertical line. All compared Chinese methods use the same reviewed annotations and recognition preprocessing; horizontal text retains the original line-level crops.

sections.heading: Computational cost.
sections.text: GPU-s/img is the summed GPU generation time divided by the number of images. Batch sizes are chosen to keep GPU compute units fully occupied throughout generation. Parameter counts include the generation network, VAE, and text encoders. Generation networks include control branches and unmerged adapters. On one NVIDIA H800, we time batch-one requests for 32 evenly spaced images from Text Refinement Bench, with two warm-up runs per implementation and three measurements per image. PixText + MeanFlow averages 1.152 s per request; batching the conditional and unconditional CFG branches reduces this to 1.062 s (7.8% faster). Even with one image per request, PixText + MeanFlow remains faster than all compared baselines, whose lowest amortized cost is 3.126 GPU-s/img.

sections.heading: Appendix E Compact Crops and Token Savings Enabled by CCPE
sections.text: CCPE allows item crops to start independently of the main-image patch grid; only their width and height must be multiples of the patch size. Compared with expanding each text box outward to grid boundaries, this reduces the extra border area included for alignment. Figure 8 illustrates both crops for the same text region. We compare the two crop choices on 116,038 text regions from 5,000 images randomly sampled from our training dataset, using a patch size of 16 pixels. Grid alignment requires 2,923,250 item tokens, whereas CCPE requires 2,523,979, a reduction of 13.7% . Both cover the same target text; the savings come from tighter crops. Figure 8: CCPE reduces crop padding. Left and middle: the same text region with two crop boundaries; orange dashed boxes mark the original OCR regions, and the background grid has 16-pixel spacing. Right: total item tokens across 116,038 text regions.

Affiliation: Alibaba Group ( alibaba-inc.com ) Email: wangguohua@alibaba-inc.com Yiyang Chen Affiliation: Alibaba Group ( alibaba-inc.com ) Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of General Artificial Intelligence, Peking University ( pku.edu.cn ) Qing-Guo Chen Affiliation: Alibaba Group ( alibaba-inc.com ) Zhao Xu Affiliation: Alibaba Group ( alibaba-inc.com ) Weihua Luo Affiliation: Alibaba Group ( alibaba-inc.com ) Yao-Xiang Ding Affiliation: State Key Lab of CAD&CG, Zhejiang University ( zju.edu.cn ) Abstract Generated images often have coherent layouts and visual content, yet local errors in small text and complex characters still limit their readability and practical use. Scene-text refinement requires accuracy , preservation , and efficiency . Existing methods based on variational autoencoders (VAEs) can lose fine strokes during reconstruction, while full-image editing can shift background colors. In this work, we introduce PixText , a model that formulates local text refinement as grouped image generation in pixel space. Conditioned on the original image, PixText generates only the target regions, preserves unedited content, and uses MeanFlow for four-step generation. We further introduce Text Refinement Bench to evaluate text correction and image preservation in generated images. On this benchmark, PixText achieves 83.06% glyph pass and 94.66% exact target-character OCR accuracy, versus 36.77% and 52.31% for the strongest baseline. Its four-step MeanFlow variant retains an 81.84% pass rate with less than one GPU-second of amortized generation cost per image. $\dagger$ $\dagger$ footnotetext: Work done during the internship at Alibaba Cloud Computing. 1 Introduction Large text-to-image models have made rapid progress in text rendering and layout. Images often exhibit reasonable layouts and mostly correct text, yet errors persist in small text and complex characters. These errors occupy only a small part of an image but directly affect its readability and practical usability. Further improving text accuracy within a general-purpose generative model requires balancing text fidelity against overall visual quality. For example, the pretraining experience of LongCat-Image shows that synthetic text data improves text accuracy but can impair overall visual coherence, motivating dynamic adjustment of its sampling proportion and its removal toward the end of pretraining ( Team et al., 2025 ) . Post-training for text accuracy faces a similar challenge: excessive optimization of text rewards can make text disproportionately large or prominent, compromising aesthetics and visual coherence ( Diao et al., 2026 ; Team et al., 2026 ; Mao et al., 2026b ; Jin et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026a ; Kang et al., 2026 ) . These observations motivate separating text refinement from overall image generation : preserving the layout, style, and visual content produced by the base model while precisely correcting only the erroneous text regions. Scene-text refinement calls for accuracy, preservation, and efficiency : correcting text faithfully, leaving unedited content unchanged, and keeping computational cost low. Existing text generation and editing methods, however, typically redraw entire text regions and can alter their original layout, style, and typeface. Most build on large latent-space generative models ( Tuo et al., 2024b ; Tuo et al., 2024a ; Lan et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) , whose ability to generate and refine small text is constrained by variational autoencoder (VAE) reconstruction ( Yu et al., 2026 ) , while also incurring the cost of a large generative network and VAE encoding and decoding. Applying these methods directly to localized corrections of a few characters therefore makes it difficult to satisfy all three requirements. To tackle these challenges, we introduce PixText , a text generation and refinement model based on grouped image generation in pixel space. First, we model images directly in pixel space, removing the VAE reconstruction bottleneck for small-character strokes as well as the texture degradation and color shifts introduced by local encoding and decoding. Second, we use the original image as the source that provides context and organize the regions to be refined as a group of image elements. The model predicts only the item pixels, which are then pasted back into the original image. By avoiding full-image regeneration, this design preserves unedited regions and reduces the background color drift and paste seams introduced by full-image generation. Finally, four-step MeanFlow ( Geng et al., 2026a ) reduces amortized generation cost to less than one GPU-second per image. Meanwhile, we propose simple, effective training and inference improvements. We identify the influence of the training timestep distribution on patch-boundary artifacts and mitigate them with uniform sampling, observing consistent improvements in our model and MiniT2I ( Wang et al., 2026d ) . We also revise the x x -prediction sampling update to reduce speckle from incomplete denoising. As a final contribution, we propose a new benchmark for text refinement. The existing AnyText Bench ( Tuo et al., 2024b ) primarily evaluates conventional text generation and lacks a dedicated evaluation of localized text errors in generated images. We therefore construct Text Refinement Bench from model-generated images, providing character-level error annotations, correction targets, and a unified evaluation protocol. The benchmark evaluates correction accuracy, background preservation, and inference efficiency. Experiments show that PixText outperforms existing baselines on text refinement and achieves performance close to or above the best existing methods on AnyText Bench at lower computational cost. 2 Related Work 2.1 Scene-Text Generation and Editing Early scene-text editing methods modeled content and style to replace text while preserving its appearance ( Wu et al., 2019 ; Roy et al., 2020 ; Yang et al., 2020 ; Krishnan et al., 2023 ; Lee et al., 2021 ; Qu et al., 2023 ) . Diffusion models improved text generation and editing through layout, glyph, and character conditioning ( Chen et al., 2023b ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2023 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024a ; Liu et al., 2024b ; Tuo et al., 2024b ; Tuo et al., 2024a ; Ji et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023a ; Zhao and Lian, 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) . Subsequent work advanced glyph accuracy, style control, and multilingual editing ( Zeng et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Yan et al., 2025 ; Fang et al., 2025 ; Lan et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026c ) , extending to open-vocabulary, training-free, and instruction-driven unified text editing ( Li et al., 2026a ; Gunawan et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026c ; Wang et al., 2026c ; Ma et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026a ) , as well as text correction in generated images ( Shimoda et al., 2025 ) . We focus on refining a few erroneous characters in generated images: jointly generating multiple target regions directly in pixel space avoids the effects of VAE compression and reconstruction on fine strokes while preserving unedited content. Four-step MeanFlow improves efficiency while keeping the amortized generation cost below one GPU-second per image. 2.2 Pixel-Space Generation Pixel-space generation models images directly, avoiding information loss from latent compression. Early work explored high-resolution modeling and computational efficiency ( Hoogeboom et al., 2023 ; Hoogeboom et al., 2025 ; Jabri et al., 2022 ; Crowson et al., 2024 ; Atzmon et al., 2024 ) , while subsequent methods improved quality and efficiency through global–local modeling and frequency decomposition ( Chen et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Yu et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026e ; Ma et al., 2026b ; Lin et al., 2026a ) . JiT demonstrated the effectiveness of predicting clean images directly ( Li and He, 2026 ) ; related studies explored perceptual supervision, generative trajectories, and text-to-image generation and editing ( Ma et al., 2026c ; Baade et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026d ; Cai et al., 2026 ) , while transferring pretrained latent-space models reduced training costs ( Chen et al., 2026d ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) . Meanwhile, MeanFlow and its successors model average velocity for few-step generation, extending this approach to pixel space ( Geng et al., 2026a ; Geng et al., 2026b ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . Building on these advances, we focus on local text refinement conditioned on the original image, jointly generating the target regions to combine glyph accuracy, content preservation, and efficiency. 3 Method Figure 1: Overview of PixText. A main image provides context, noisy item images represent the regions to be generated, and glyph images specify the target text. Position encoding aligns each item and its glyph with the main image. Group JiT blocks predict the item pixels, which are composed into the original image. 3.1 Pixel-Space Generation for Quality and Efficiency Latent-space text generation and editing methods rely on VAE compression and reconstruction ( Li et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2023b ; Zeng et al., 2024 ; Tuo et al., 2024b ; Tuo et al., 2024a ; Lan et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) , which can lose fine strokes and incur additional decoding cost. Related work on autoregressive models also identifies visual-tokenizer reconstruction as a bottleneck for text detail and improves glyph quality by enhancing the decoder ( Mao et al., 2026a ) . In Figure 2 , a character approximately 20 pixels high becomes difficult to recognize after reconstruction with Stable Diffusion, FLUX.1, and Qwen-Image VAEs ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Labs et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) . For edits involving only a few characters, decoding only the target region may lower VAE decoding cost, but the smaller region gives the decoder less image context. Figure 3 compares full-image and local FLUX.1-VAE decoding from the same latent representation obtained by encoding the full image: the independently decoded region exhibits a visible color mismatch when pasted back, even with 32 pixels of additional context. Figure 2: Small-character degradation during VAE reconstruction. Each VAE uses full-image encoding and posterior-mode decoding in FP32. Figure 3: Local FLUX.1-VAE decoding causes visible color shifts when pasted back into the original image, even with 32 pixels of context. We therefore build a flow matching model directly in pixel space, eliminating VAE encoding and decoding, and adopt the simple JiT architecture ( Li and He, 2026 ) . Recent scene-text editing methods ( Lan et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ) use full-image inpainting: even for local text edits, they update and decode full-image latents, reconstructing background that requires no modification. This full-image generation can shift background colors, leaving visible seams after crop-and-paste editing ( Figure 4 (a) ). The shift exceeds the VAE-only reconstruction error, showing that pasting alone does not ensure color consistency between the edited region and the original image. We formulate text editing and refinement as grouped image generation in pixel space, separating context from generation targets. During both training and inference, we erase the existing text in each target region through local blurring before using the source image as the main-image condition. The resulting image serves as a main image providing context, while each region to be edited forms an item image . The model predicts only the item pixels and pastes them into the original. The extent of generation therefore follows the size of the edit regions, while pixels outside them are retained directly. We denote the N N clean items by x 1 = { x 1 i } i = 1 N x_{1}=\{x_{1}^{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} and their noisy counterparts by z t = { z t i } i = 1 N z_{t}=\{z_{t}^{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} . Conditioned on the main image and target glyph images, denoted by c c , the model jointly predicts x ^ 1 = f θ ​ ( z t , t , c ) \hat{x}_{1}=f_{\theta}(z_{t},t,c) . The input comprises main-image, noisy item-image, and glyph-image tokens, which provide scene context, represent generation targets, and specify text content, respectively. At sampling time, item images are initialized from 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{N}(0,I) . Main and item images share an RGB embedder. Glyph images are rendered with PIL in single-channel grayscale and mapped to the same feature dimension through a separate glyph embedder. Target text is specified entirely through these glyph images, removing the need to deploy an additional text encoder. As illustrated in Figure 1 (b) , we use Centered Continuous Position Encoding (CCPE) to align the main image and independently cropped items across scales in the coordinate system of the original image. Let the original image have size H × W H\times W , the patch size be p p , and ( y , x ) (y,x) denote a patch center in original-image pixel coordinates. Across 116,038 text regions, this reduces the number of item tokens by 13.7% relative to grid-aligned crops; Appendix E provides the comparison. We adapt JiT blocks for grouped image generation and call the resulting blocks Group JiT Blocks . These tokens are jointly processed by 32 such blocks. As illustrated in Figure 1 (c) , the main image and items interact bidirectionally, and different items attend to one another to share scene information and editing context. We therefore construct Text Refinement Bench from actual model-generated images, including those released in the public Qwen-Image Bench ( Li et al., 2026b ) . Human review verifies erroneous character regions and correction targets and excludes invalid cases before freezing the evaluation list, directly reflecting the practical need to correct local errors while preserving the original image. The benchmark evaluates correction accuracy and image preservation on 1,034 images with 2,638 repair targets. We also evaluate text reconstruction on the Chinese and English subsets of AnyText Bench to assess performance on conventional visual text generation. During evaluation, we identify inaccurate text polygons and failures of the original OCR evaluation pipeline on vertically arranged text. We correct the affected text regions and adapt OCR preprocessing for vertical layouts, reducing scoring errors caused by cropping and text orientation so that evaluation better reflects the quality of the generated text. Standard OCR may transcribe a generated glyph with missing or extra strokes as the intended character, so correct recognition does not necessarily imply a successful repair. We therefore use CJK-CLIP, a dedicated CLIP-style glyph recognizer for characters, 1 1 1 The work presenting CJK-CLIP is currently under review; the model will be publicly released. to distinguish correct glyphs from visually similar but structurally incorrect outputs for character-level evaluation on Text Refinement Bench. Appendix D further describes the benchmark, its differences from related benchmarks, and the evaluation protocol. Implementation details. We train the model on eight H800 GPUs using an internal Chinese–English dataset containing approximately 2.53 million image records. Base-model training uses AdamW with a learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} , β = ( 0.9 , 0.95 ) \beta=(0.9,0.95) , zero weight decay, and an EMA decay of 0.9999. Each optimizer reinitialization starts with 2,000 linear warmup steps, followed by a constant learning rate. We follow a progressive-resolution schedule: we first train for approximately 13 epochs with at most 512 2 512^{2} pixels per main image, then increase this limit to 1024 2 1024^{2} and continue training for approximately 15 epochs. We subsequently perform approximately 3,000 MeanFlow updates with an effective batch size of 24. PixText uses patch size p = 16 p=16 , 32 Group JiT Blocks, hidden dimension 1280, and 16 attention heads. The denominator floor for velocity conversion is δ = 0.05 \delta=0.05 . Initial logit-normal timestep sampling uses μ = − 0.8 \mu=-0.8 and σ = 0.8 \sigma=0.8 , followed by uniform sampling. MeanFlow uses the same optimizer settings. Both the student and frozen teacher are initialized from the base model’s EMA weights, and training intervals are formed by sorting two independently sampled uniform timesteps. The default DDE step size is h = 0.005 h=0.005 , reduced near boundaries as described above. Finite-difference predictions and subtraction use FP32 tensor arithmetic, with TF32 enabled for matrix multiplications; the trainable student forward and backward passes use BF16 mixed precision. For the main-table evaluation, PixText uses 25 Euler steps and MeanFlow uses four Euler steps, both with a glyph-conditioned classifier-free guidance (CFG) ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) scale of 3.3 (see Appendix B for details). 4.2 Quantitative Comparisons Table 2 compares eight text-specialized methods with PixText and its four-step MeanFlow variant. On Text Refinement Bench, PixText achieves a Pass of 83.06%, compared with 36.77% for the strongest baseline, FLUX-Text, while also attaining the lowest FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) and LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) . PP-OCRv6 gives PixText 94.66% exact target-character accuracy, compared with 52.31% for FLUX-Text. On AnyText Bench, PixText achieves the highest Chinese text accuracy and ranks second to FLUX-Text on English, showing that its refinement advantage is accompanied by competitive text reconstruction. For each Chinese-capable baseline, we report the complete line- or character-input run with higher text accuracy; Table 4 reports both settings and all four metrics. The four-step MeanFlow variant retains the refinement advantage over the baselines while reducing generation cost relative to the base PixText model, making localized correction practical in generation workflows.
